citation: [A survey of the residences of Prairie Avenue, Sixteenth to Twenty-second Street, west side then east side, beginning 'Chicago has every reason to be proud of her beautiful homes.'] The Daily Inter Ocean (Chicago), 2 January 1887; transcribed on chicagology.com, Prairie Avenue page, under the heading 'Inter Ocean, January 2, 1887'.
author: unsigned
describes_date: 1886-1887 (winter: the Glessner and O. R. Keith houses not yet finished)
repository: The Daily Inter Ocean; read only in chicagology.com's transcription. The project's extract of the same text for 1620 Prairie is inter_ocean_1887_1620_prairie_olive_green.
locator: The transcription's paragraphs on Shortall (the first house south of Sixteenth Street, west side), 1620 Law, 1628 Einstein, the Glessner house (south-west corner of Eighteenth Street), the Allerton house, 1721 Dexter and the Pullman grounds, the unimproved east frontage south of Eighteenth Street, and the Field house. The issue's page and column are not known here.
rights_note: The Inter Ocean, 1887: a United States imprint long out of copyright. Quoted in text only.

note: Read (transcription): of Shortall's house, 'The grounds are enclosed with an iron fence.' Of 1620: 'The house is commodious, olive green in color, and affords a fine view of the lake.' Of 1628: 'His own residence, No. 1628, is a three-story pressed-brick front, which stands back in well-kept grounds.' Of the Glessner house: 'There is no dividing line between the outer walls of the house and stable. ... The house covers every foot of the frontage. The grounds within are not visible except from the house of the owner.' Of Allerton's: 'The Allerton mansion is conspicuous for its size and the extent of the grounds attached to it. ... this fine residence is especially noticeable because of its unrivaled grounds. Some ideas may be gained of their value when it is known that Mr. Allerton refused $117,000 for the lawn south of his home.' Of 1721: 'Only an imaginary dividing line separates the grounds of Mr. Wirt Dexter and his friend, Mr. George M. Pullman'. South of Eighteenth Street: 'Crossing Eighteenth street, there is a long east frontage of unimproved lots.' Of Field's: 'Upon the southern exposure is a conservatory fitted with rare flowers.' Seventeen years before the scene date, and from a transcription.

unimproved lots on the east side south of Eighteenth Street in winter 1886-87
